speaker_role: former admissions officer (former director of admissions, Swarthmore; former AO, Vanderbilt)
commercial_incentive: Yes - promotes a paid application-review service and a paid 'parents ultimate college admissions course'
key_insights: For 2026, several schools newly added or expanded early programs (e.g. WashU adding EA, Occidental and Connecticut College adding EA, Chapman adding ED2, USC adding ED for most programs, Florida and Florida State adding ED/ED for domestic students), showing policies change yearly and must be checked directly

Colleges expand early programs strategically to improve yield predictability, compete with peers, identify committed students sooner, or otherwise shape the incoming class, not just as a minor administrative tweak

Restrictive/single-choice early action bars applying early action to other private schools simultaneously (e.g. can't do EA at both Harvard and Yale) and is enforceable because the counselor sends only one early transcript
ED2 has a later deadline (around Jan 1-15) and functions as a second binding option, generally more competitive since it draws students whose ED1 didn't work out

Speaker states ED's higher acceptance rate isn't because it's objectively 'easier' but because admissions committees prioritize yield certainty and are simultaneously building a balanced class (by major, income level, geographic/talent needs, etc.), not evaluating students purely in isolation

ED is an ethical agreement co-signed by student, parent, and counselor, not a legal contract, but violating it (e.g. not withdrawing other applications after enrolling) can lead admissions offices to jointly detect the breach and rescind the offer, as in a case the speaker personally handled

Legitimate exit from an ED agreement is financial: families should complete the college's net price calculator beforehand, and if the actual awarded aid is substantially worse, they can appeal to financial aid before considering withdrawal

Speaker's framework: decide where you would unquestionably enroll if admitted (not just 'where can I apply early'), and only commit to ED once research, financial modeling, and application readiness are all in place; casting a wide net of 30-40 schools rather than fixating only on the most famous names is recommended
specific_numbers_or_facts: Named 2026-cycle changes: WashU St. Louis adds EA; Occidental College and Connecticut College add EA; Chapman University adds ED2; USC adds ED for most programs; University of Florida adds ED; Florida State adds ED for domestic applicants
ED2 deadlines typically cited as around January 1st-15th
National enrollment reply deadline cited as typically May 1st
Speaker's example case: a Barnard ED admit initially facing about $40,000/year was appealed down to under $5,000/year in family contribution after providing documentation
notable_or_distinctive: Gives an insider explanation of why ED acceptance rates are higher (class-building/yield management, not lower bar) and a real rescinded-offer anecdote from the speaker's own admissions career illustrating enforcement of the ED ethical agreement.
reliability_notes: Speaker has verifiable named credentials (former Swarthmore admissions director, former Vanderbilt AO) lending credibility, though the video promotes paid services; specific 2026-cycle policy changes should be verified against current college websites since they can shift after publication.
